newsitem.title: UK: Britain protests to China over Hong Kong plans.
newsitem.headline: Britain protests to China over Hong Kong plans.

text.p: Britain lodged a strong protest with China on Wednesday over Beijing's plans to dilute laws guaranteeing civil liberties in Hong Kong when it regains control of the British colony later this year.
The Foreign Office said junior minister Jeremy Hanley expressed Britain's "serious concern" over the proposals at a meeting with Chinese ambassador Jiang Enzhu.

A spokesman said Hanley told the envoy that Hong Kong's bill of rights and related legislation, which China wants to amend, were fully consistent with the Basic Law -- the post-1997 constitution for Hong Kong promulgated by Beijing in 1990.
They were also in line with the U.N. Covenant on Civil and Political Rights and with the Sino-British Joint Declaration, the treaty which governs Hong Kong's handover, Hanley insisted.
"We see no need or justification for changing them. The proposal to do so has caused widespread dismay in Hong Kong and around the world," the Foreign Office spokesman said.

China, which said the matter was an internal affair, is moving to replace Hong Kong's elected Legislative Council with a provisional legislature and to block a lenient British law that would exclude China-style crackdowns on dissent.
China's opponents say these steps fly in the face of vows that allow Hong Kong to keep its freedoms after it becomes a Special Administrative Region of China.
The United States expressed strong concern on Tuesday and called on China to reconsider.
"Statements and recommendations of this kind do not help foster stability or confidence in Hong Kong," State Department spokesman Nicholas Burns said on Tuesday.

"We hope that China and the future Hong Kong government will consider seriously the damage that erosion of Hong Kong's civil liberties and basic freedoms could do to its way of life and its high degree of autonomy," he added.

Foreign Office officials said Jiang gave China's standard explanation that it needed to amend the legislation because Britain had introduced it without consulting Beijing. They said he also undertook to report Britain's views to his government.
Britain will now follow up Wednesday's protest by raising the issues at the Joint Liaison Group, a forum in which Chinese and British diplomats meet regularly to thrash out transitional issues.
China's intention of amending or repealing a list of 25 laws and ordinances has ignited a storm of protest in Hong Kong.

Governor Chris Patten called Beijing's move a "legal nonsense" while pro-democracy groups said it was a blow to democracy and human rights that would dent overseas confidence in Hong Kong beyond the handover at midnight on June 30.
Earlier on Wednesday Hong Kong's post-colonial leader, Tung Chee-hwa, who takes over from Governor Chris Patten on July 1, called for calm.
"I think we are being too dramatic," Tung told Hong Kong radio. "It is a very complex issue," he said.
